title: Yuksom and the 1642 crowning of Sikkim's first king
meta_description: How three lamas crowned Phuntsog Namgyal at Norbugang, Yuksom, in 1642, what still stands at the coronation throne, Kathok Lake and Dubdi, and how to visit.
summary: In 1642 three Tibetan lamas crowned Phuntsog Namgyal as the first Chogyal of Sikkim at Norbugang in Yuksom. The stone throne, the Norbugang Chorten, Kathok Lake and the Dubdi Monastery above the village still stand, and you can walk to all of them from Yuksom in a day for little or no cost.

sections.heading: Before the kingdom
paras: Long before there was a Sikkim on any map, the hills between the Singalila ridge and the Teesta were home to the Lepcha, who call the land Mayel Lyang, and to Limbu and other Kirati peoples further west. Tibetan settlers had been coming over the passes for centuries, and Buddhism of the Nyingma school had a foothold by the 1600s. Sikkimese tradition remembers an earlier pact, sworn at Kabi in North Sikkim, between the Lepcha elder Thekong Tek and the Tibetan prince Khye Bumsa, with Kangchenjunga as witness.
What Sikkim did not yet have was a single ruler. That changed in the Rathong Chu valley, in a basin of forest and terraced fields at about 1,780 m, which is now the village of Yuksom.

sections.heading: Three lamas meet at Yuksom
paras: In 1641–42 three Nyingma lamas travelled into Sikkim from Tibet, each by a different route. They were Lhatsun Chenpo (Lhatsun Namkha Jigme), Ngadak Sempa Chenpo and Kathok Rigzin Chenpo. Wikipedia's account of Sikkim's history describes them as coming from the north, west and south, and says the Lepcha name of the place where they met, Yuksom, means 'the place where the three monks met': a lama is 'yukmun' in Lepcha, and three is 'som'.

Their purpose, as the tradition tells it, was to open the hidden land of Demazong, the 'valley of rice', blessed by Guru Padmasambhava, and to find the man who would rule it as a religious king. Three had come; the prophecy called for a fourth, from the east.

Each lama brought his own lineage within the Nyingma school, and each is remembered at a different monastery. That is one reason why the monasteries of West Sikkim feel so closely linked: they grew from the same moment, among the same small group of teachers, in the same few years of the 1640s. When you visit Dubdi, Pemayangtse and Tashiding, you are visiting the foundations of those three men.

sections.heading: The man churning milk
paras: Here history and legend run side by side, and we should say which is which. Tradition holds that the lamas sent messengers east and found a man near present-day Gangtok churning milk. He offered them refreshment and shelter, and they took this, with signs of his descent from Khye Bumsa's line, as proof that he was the chosen one. His name was Phuntsog.

The record is firmer on what happened next. In 1642 Phuntsog Namgyal, then 38 years old, was brought to Yuksom and consecrated as the first Chogyal, the 'righteous king', on a stone seat set under a pine on a hill at Norbugang, and anointed with water from a sacred urn. Lhatsun Chenpo gave him the name Namgyal. The dynasty he founded ruled Sikkim, through twelve kings, until 1975.

sections.heading: What you can see today
paras: Norbugang is a short walk from Yuksom's main road, inside a small park with a prayer hall and a large prayer wheel. The coronation throne is a tiered platform of whitewashed stones with four seats; the highest was for Lhatsun Chenpo, the others for the two lamas and the king. It sits beneath a huge old cryptomeria. Opposite stands the Norbugang Chorten, which, according to the accounts, the lamas built from earth and stones gathered from every part of Sikkim, sealing inside it the gifts the people had brought to the ceremony.

A stone near the throne shows what is said to be the footprint of one of the lamas. Down the lane, Kathok Lake is a small, quiet pond ringed with prayer flags; its water, tradition says, was used for the consecration. On the hill above the village, about an hour's walk, Dubdi Monastery was established in 1701 and is described as the oldest surviving monastery in Sikkim. Images of the three lamas are kept inside.

None of this is behind glass. There is no museum, no audio guide and, usually, no ticket. The throne is simply there, a little worn, often draped with white scarves left by pilgrims. That plainness is part of what makes Norbugang moving. Sit for a few minutes, look up at the old tree, and remember that a kingdom that lasted more than three centuries began on this patch of ground.

sections.heading: From Yuksom to Rabdentse and beyond
paras: Phuntsog Namgyal made Yuksom his capital and set up Sikkim's first central administration, dividing the kingdom into twelve districts, or dzongs, under Lepcha governors. His reign is also credited with the idea of Lho-Mon-Tsong-Sum, the unity of the Bhutia, Lepcha and Limbu communities, formalised in 1663. He died in 1670, and his son Tensung Namgyal moved the court to Rabdentse, on the ridge near today's Pelling, ending Yuksom's time as capital.

Each of the three lamas left a foundation of his own. Lhatsun Chenpo is linked with Dubdi and with Pemayangtse, begun in 1647. Ngadak Sempa Chenpo is remembered at Tashiding, where the Bumchu vase is kept. Together these places form the old pilgrimage circuit of West Sikkim, and Yuksom sits at its head.

sections.heading: Yuksom today
paras: Yuksom is still small: about 1,950 people at the 2011 census, mostly Bhutia and Nepali families, living along one main road and the lanes that branch off it. The visitors often outnumber the residents in October, when trekking groups come and go from the Goecha La trail, but for most of the year the village is quiet. Cows wander past the coronation park, children walk to school in uniform, and the evening smells of wood smoke and frying momos.

The village has looked after its own landscape. The Khangchendzonga Conservation Committee, based in Yuksom, has worked with the forest department on clean-up drives along the trek and on homestays that keep tourism money in local hands. If you stay in a homestay, eat local food and walk rather than drive between the sites, you are travelling the way the village has asked visitors to travel.

sections.heading: How to visit
paras: Yuksom is about 35 km and 1.5–2 hours from Pelling, and about 150 km and 6–7 hours from Siliguri. Shared jeeps run from Gyalshing for about ₹120–180 a seat, indicative 2026; a reserved car from Pelling costs ₹2,000–2,800 one way. We suggest two nights: arrive in the afternoon, walk to Norbugang and Kathok Lake the next morning, climb to Dubdi before lunch, and keep the following morning for Tashiding on the way out.

Go early. In the first hour after sunrise the Norbugang park is usually empty, the light falls softly through the cryptomeria, and you can sit by the throne without a crowd. Walk clockwise around the chorten and the prayer wheels, keep your voice low, and do not climb on the throne. Dubdi is sometimes locked when its caretaker monk is away; ask in the village before you climb. Check current status before you travel.
list: Best months: October–December and March–May; January–February are cold but clear.
Stay: Hotel Yangrigang on the main road, or one of the village homestays.
Wear proper shoes for the Dubdi path, which is steep and slippery after rain.
Carry cash; Yuksom has limited ATM access.

faqs.q: Who was the first king of Sikkim
faqs.a: Phuntsog Namgyal (1604–1670), crowned as the first Chogyal of Sikkim at Norbugang in Yuksom in 1642, at the age of 38. He was consecrated by three Tibetan lamas, Lhatsun Chenpo, Ngadak Sempa Chenpo and Kathok Rigzin Chenpo. His Namgyal dynasty ruled Sikkim until 1975, when the kingdom became a state of India.

Yuksom is a Lepcha name usually explained as 'the place where the three monks met', from 'yukmun', a lama, and 'som', three, referring to the three lamas who met there and crowned the first Chogyal in 1642. You will also see it written Yuksam. It was Sikkim's first capital, from 1642 until 1670.

faqs.q: Where is the coronation throne of the first Chogyal
faqs.a: At Norbugang, a short walk from Yuksom's main road, in a small park with a prayer hall and prayer wheel. The whitewashed stone throne has four seats, the highest for Lhatsun Chenpo, and stands under a large old cryptomeria. Opposite is the Norbugang Chorten. Entry is free.

faqs.q: Is the story of the man churning milk true
faqs.a: It is tradition, not documented history. Sikkimese accounts say the lamas found Phuntsog near present-day Gangtok churning milk and recognised him by his hospitality and his descent from Khye Bumsa. The coronation at Norbugang in 1642 itself is well recorded. We tell the milk-churning story as legend.

faqs.q: Which is the oldest monastery in Sikkim
faqs.a: Dubdi Monastery, on a hill about 3 km above Yuksom, established in 1701, is described as the oldest surviving monastery in Sikkim. It is linked with Lhatsun Chenpo and holds images of the three lamas. The walk up takes about an hour. Ask in the village whether the caretaker is there before you go.

faqs.q: How long should I stay in Yuksom
faqs.a: Two nights is ideal for a non-trekker: one morning for Norbugang and Kathok Lake, another for Dubdi Monastery, and a half day for Tashiding on the way out. Trekkers heading to Goecha La usually spend one night before and one after the trek here. Yuksom is quiet, so bring a book.

faqs.q: How do I get to Yuksom from Pelling
faqs.a: By reserved car, about 35 km and 1.5–2 hours, for ₹2,000–2,800 one way, indicative 2026; many people add Khecheopalri Lake and the waterfalls on the way. By shared jeep, go down to Gyalshing and take the midday Yuksom jeep for ₹120–180. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Why did Sikkim's capital move from Yuksom to Rabdentse
faqs.a: In 1670 the second Chogyal, Tensung Namgyal, moved the court to Rabdentse, a ridge near today's Pelling. Wikipedia's accounts record the move without a detailed reason. Rabdentse remained the capital until 1814 and was later destroyed in the wars with Nepal. Its ruins are an easy walk from Pelling.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee at Norbugang and Dubdi
faqs.a: No fixed fee has applied at Norbugang, Kathok Lake or Dubdi Monastery, though donations at the monastery are welcome. Some sites in Sikkim have introduced small charges in recent years, so carry a little cash and check current status before you travel. Photography is usually allowed outside but ask before shooting inside temples.
